body:
N-40 MEASURED ON A REAL PHONE, 26 Nov 2026 (lead; the advisor's measure-first step; NOTHING BUILT, no production code). Phone: the A35 (Samsung, One UI 8.0, Android 16), APK build 162 (main b575189), VM 108 on sha-b575189 (homelab log entries 12, 13). Setup: the owner's test download "'00s Hip Hop" (189 songs, 770 MB, all 188 available songs already kept on the server: no YouTube look-up involved) was removed on the phone and downloaded again; battery 100% on USB, standby bucket 'active', Encore not in the battery-optimisation whitelist, no foreground service (0 found). The app was swiped away from the recents screen with a fling (NOT `am force-stop`).
WHAT WAS SEEN. (1) Before the swipe: about 1.0 to 1.25 MB/s received on Wi-Fi (the phone is otherwise idle; read from /proc/net/dev every 5 s), 35 of 189 songs on the phone about 80 s after the start. (2) The swipe at 10:01:28 UTC KILLED the process (ps: gone) and the bytes stopped within 5 s: 0.03 MB/s in the next sample, then 0.00. From the swipe to the reopen 3 minutes later only 0.27 MB arrived in total, less than one song (a song is about 4 MB): so the file in flight did NOT finish either, which is worse than the item note's 'the files in flight finish'. (3) Nothing restarted by itself in those 3 minutes (no process, 0 bytes). (4) Reopening the app (10:04:30) restarted the downloads within about 5 s and the rate was back to 1.24 MB/s.
SO: today a download lives and dies with the app's process; swiping Encore away stops it, with about 150 of 189 songs still to come, and it resumes only when the person opens the app. The note's premise is proved; what the note said about the files in flight was too kind. NOT measured: other One UI battery settings, a phone on battery rather than USB, Android 14/15 dataSync limits, the background sync job (15 minutes), a swipe while the screen is off.
DESIGN QUESTION FOR THE ADVISOR (nothing is built): a foreground service of type dataSync (Android 15 caps it at 6 h per 24 h) or a user-initiated data-transfer job (Android 14+), with its own notification, and how N-45 (a task id per attempt, a migration of the phone's database) travels with it. The reviewer-attacker is warranted only for N-45's migration.
Tools: handoff-2026-11-03/scripts/session-26nov/n40_net.py (bytes and process every 5 s), n40_sample.py; data: local/n40-measure/ (net.txt, swipe_time.txt, reopen_time.txt).
